title: Academic Integrity at University

keyTerms.definition: being honest and responsible in your studies
using someone else's words or ideas as your own, without saying where they came from
working together on a task that should be done alone
a note that shows where you found an idea or words

predictionQuestion: What do you think "academic integrity" means? What rules might the lecturer talk about?

segments.text: Hello, everyone. Today we're going to talk about academic integrity. Academic integrity means being honest and responsible in your studies. It means that the work you hand in is your own, and that you give credit to other people whose ideas or words you use. In this talk, I want to cover three points: why integrity matters, the most common forms of misconduct, and how you can protect yourself.

So, first, why does it matter? A university degree is a kind of promise. It tells employers and the public that the graduate has the knowledge and skills that the degree describes. If students hand in work that is not their own, that promise becomes meaningless. Integrity also matters for you personally. The purpose of an assignment is to help you learn. If someone else does the thinking, you miss the learning.

Now, let's look at the most common forms of misconduct. The best known is plagiarism. Plagiarism means presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, without acknowledging them. It also includes paraphrasing, that is, changing the words but keeping the ideas, without giving a reference.

A second form is collusion. Collusion happens when students work together on a task that is supposed to be done individually. For example, two students who write an essay together, and both submit it as their own work. A third form is contract cheating, which means getting another person or a company to complete your work for you. Using an AI tool to write work that you then submit as your own may also break the rules, depending on your university's policy, so always check.

The important thing to remember is that misconduct is not always deliberate. Many students break the rules by accident, often because they are not sure how to reference properly, or because they are under time pressure. Unfortunately, not knowing the rules is usually not accepted as an excuse.

So, how can you protect yourself? Here are three habits. One, keep careful notes of your sources while you research, so you always know where an idea came from. Two, learn the referencing style your course uses, and use it every time. And three, plan your time. If you're unsure about anything, ask your lecturer or the library for help.

Right, to wrap up. Academic integrity means being honest about whose work and ideas you are using. It matters because it protects the value of your degree, and your own learning. The main forms of misconduct are plagiarism, collusion and contract cheating. And the best protection is good habits: record your sources, reference carefully, and manage your time.

keyIdeas.text: Academic integrity means being honest: your work is your own, and you give credit to others.
It matters because a degree is a promise to employers and the public.
It also matters for you: assignments help you learn. If someone else thinks, you miss the learning.
Plagiarism: presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without acknowledging them.
Paraphrasing without a reference is also plagiarism.
Collusion: students working together on a task that should be done alone.
Contract cheating: getting a person or company to do your work. AI use may also break the rules, so check.
Misconduct is not always deliberate, but not knowing the rules is usually not an excuse.
You can protect yourself with good habits.
Habits: keep notes of sources, learn your referencing style, plan your time, and ask for help.

modelNotes: ACADEMIC INTEGRITY = honest + responsible: own work, credit others' ideas/words
- degree = promise to employers + public (knowledge + skills)
- for you: assignment → learning; s.o. else thinks → no learning
- plagiarism: others' words/ideas as own, no acknowledgement (incl. paraphrase w/o ref.)
- collusion: work together on individual task (e.g. 2 students, 1 essay)
- contract cheating: person/company does your work; AI? → check uni policy
- often NOT deliberate (unsure how to ref., time pressure) BUT not knowing ≠ excuse
- learn referencing style → use every time
- plan time; unsure? ask lecturer / library
